etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English cerymonye, from Latin caerimonia or caeremonia, later often cerimonia (“sacredness, reverence, a sacred rite”).

definitions.definition: A ritual, with religious or cultural significance.

quote.citation: 1596, Edmund Spenser, “Book VI, Canto VIII”, in The Faerie Queene. […], London:  […]  [John Wolfe] for William Ponsonbie, →OCLC, pages 463-464:
quote.text: To whom the Priest with naked armes full netApproching nigh, and murdrous knife well whet,Gan mutter close a certaine secret charme,With other diuelish ceremonies met:

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Numbers 9:3:
quote.text: In the fourteenth day of this month, at even, ye shall keep [the passover] in his appointed season: according to all the rites of it, and according to all the ceremonies thereof, shall ye keep it.

quote.citation: 1881, Henry James, Jr., chapter 1, in The Portrait of a Lady, New York, N.Y.: Houghton, Mifflin and Company […], →OCLC, page 1:
quote.text: Under certain circumstances there are few hours in life more agreeable than the hour dedicated to the ceremony known as afternoon tea.

definitions.definition: An official gathering to celebrate, commemorate, or otherwise mark some event.
(uncountable) A formal socially established behaviour, often in relation to people of different ranks; formality.

quote.citation: c. 1606 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of Macbeth”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act III, scene iv]:
quote.text: […]  to feed were best at home;From thence the sauce to meat is ceremony;Meeting were bare without it.

quote.citation: 1928, W. Somerset Maugham, “Miss King”, in Ashenden‎[1], New York: Avon, published 1943, page 37:
quote.text: Monsieur Bridet, notwithstanding his costume and his evident harrassment [sic], found in himself the presence of mind to remain the attentive manager, and with ceremony effected the proper introduction.

quote.citation: 1959, C. S. Forester, Hunting the Bismarck‎[2], London: Michael Joseph:
quote.text: They went into the bars and interrupted the drinking, hustling the men out without ceremony.

quote.citation: 1667, John Milton, “Book I”, in Paradise Lost. […], London:  […]  [Samuel Simmons], and are to be sold by Peter Parker […]; [a]nd by Robert Boulter […]; [a]nd Matthias Walker, […], →OCLC; republished as Paradise Lost in Ten Books: […], London: Basil Montagu Pickering […], 1873, →OCLC, lines 752-756:
quote.text: Meanwhile the winged Heralds, by commandOf sovereign power, with awful ceremonyAnd trumpet’s sound, throughout the host proclaimA solemn council forthwith to be heldAt Pandemonium  […]

quote.citation: 1829, Washington Irving, chapter 46, in A Chronicle of the Conquest of Granada‎[3], volume II, Philadelphia: Carey, Lea & Carey, page 254:
quote.text: Immediately after her arrival, the queen rode forth to survey the camp and its environs: wherever she went, she was attended by a splendid retinue; and all the commanders vied with each other, in the pomp and ceremony with which they received her.

definitions.definition: (obsolete) An accessory or object associated with a ritual.

quote.citation: 1599 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Life of Henry the Fift”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act IV, scene i]:
quote.text: […]  his ceremonies laid by, in his nakedness he appears but a man  […]

quote.citation: c. 1603–1604 (date written), William Shakespeare, “Measure for Measure”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act II, scene ii]:
quote.text: […]  Well, believe this,No ceremony that to great ones ’longs,Not the king’s crown, nor the deputed sword,The marshal’s truncheon, nor the judge’s robe,Become them with one half so good a graceAs mercy does.

quote.citation: 1599 (first performance), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of Iulius Cæsar”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act II, scene i]:
quote.text: For he is superstitious grown of late,Quite from the main opinion he held onceOf fantasy, of dreams, and ceremonies.

quote.citation: 1599 (first performance), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of Iulius Cæsar”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act II, scene ii]:
quote.text: Caesar, I never stood on ceremonies,Yet now they fright me.
